Brazil’s National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) has ordered Discord to suspend its "Go Live" feature and all equivalent video streaming tools across the country within three business days.

The platform itself is not blocked. Text chat, voice channels and other core functions remain fully available to Brazilian users. The suspension will stay in place until Discord proves it has implemented effective safeguards to protect children and adolescents.

The decision follows an investigation into child safety failures linked to the death of a 13-year-old girl in Naviraí (Mato Grosso do Sul) on 22 July. Authorities say she was encouraged to take her own life during a roughly 45-minute private Discord livestream. Five teenagers and one 18-year-old have been arrested in connection with the case (Operation Lívia). ANPD cited Discord’s lack of real-time access to livestream content, which prevents automated detection of violations, as well as reliance on flawed systems and user reports.

First Lady Janja da Silva had publicly called for a full ban of the platform days earlier. Discord described the order as "premature," stating it is carefully reviewing the measure, continues to cooperate with law enforcement, and confirmed it quickly removed the private server involved. The company noted that some of the activity was coordinated on other platforms.

Failure to comply could result in fines of up to 50 million reais (approximately $9.7 million) per violation. Discord has 10 business days to appeal. A complete ban of the platform would still require a court decision.

My son announced on Tuesday evening, during dinner, that for Halloween he wanted to dress up as a fart.

I literally almost choked on the water I was drinking. He’s six years old. He was just sitting there, serious, with spaghetti sauce on his chin, saying: “I want to be a big brown fart cloud.” My husband looked at me like it was my job to handle the situation. I didn’t know what to say. Where do kids even get these ideas? I told him absolutely not. To pick something normal — a superhero, a dinosaur, anything else. He made that stubborn face that means “he’s never going to let this go.”

He started explaining to me, with the utmost seriousness, that farts are funny, that everyone would laugh, and that it would be the best costume ever. I was exhausted after work, my head was pounding, and I lost my patience. I said: fine. You want to be a fart? Make it yourself. I’ll help you find the materials, but the rest is up to you. I thought he’d give up after ten minutes. He didn’t.
He spent the next three days in the living room, working with brown and beige fabrics I helped him order, because apparently he needed “fart-colored tulle” — a phrase I never thought I’d say. He watched tutorials on my phone about how to gather fabric, asked me for help with the knots, but insisted on arranging every single layer himself. He got frustrated twice, was close to crying, but kept going. His little hands working carefully, his tongue between his teeth as he focused.

Yesterday he finished. He put it on and strutted around the house, proudly showing it off to his father and grandmother, who both looked absolutely stunned. I thought I’d be embarrassed, but instead I felt a strange pride. My son said he wanted to be a fart, I told him to figure it out himself, and he… actually did it.

He’s been sleeping in it for two nights. Two neighbors have already asked if I can make one for their kids, too. I told them he’s taking orders now. Eight dollars per cloud. He’s never been so confident in his life.

Walmart is selling real diamond earrings for $12.

Not a typo. Half-carat lab-grown diamonds, same carbon, graded by the same labs that grade the stone in your engagement ring. A jeweler can't tell them apart without a machine.

And that $12 price tag is why the company that invented the engagement ring is about to get sold for scrap.

De Beers ran the diamond trade for over a century. At its peak it controlled up to 90% of the world's rough supply, and when demand dipped it just locked diamonds in London vaults until prices came back. The slogan "A Diamond Is Forever" came from their ad agency in 1947. So did the rule that a ring should cost two months of your salary. Before that campaign, most American brides never got a diamond at all.

The whole thing held for 80 years because there were only so many mines. Then China started growing diamonds in reactors, and there's no vault on earth big enough to hide a factory's output.

Lab-grown wholesale prices have crashed roughly 96% from their peak, down to around $100 a carat. The Knot says 61% of engagement rings sold in 2025 had lab-grown center stones, up 239% since 2020. Even De Beers' own average selling price fell 32% in a year, to $105 a carat.

So Anglo American, which owns De Beers, has written it down by $6.8 billion in two years and is now in talks to sell the whole thing for about $1 billion. This is a company that was valued over $18 billion in 2001 and $13 billion as recently as 2011.

The stones coming out of the ground are the same as ever. The only scarce thing De Beers ever owned was the marketing, and marketing doesn't survive a $12 price tag at Walmart.

I watched the F1 film with Brad Pitt the other day, and there’s a moment where his character asks to add something to the car that isn’t really in the rules. The FIA punishes it, but the team can still race with the earlier car. It made me think.

In F1, the best teams live at the edge of the regulations. Sometimes the FIA allows what they’ve found, and sometimes it says that goes too far. Occasionally the rules are rewritten afterwards.

Now, City. I’m not defending them. A commission found they entered into sham agreements and broke the spending limits. A sham is an arrangement that isn’t what it claims to be, so that’s a different thing from using a gap nobody had spotted.

City deny it and will appeal. But I find it useful to ask/reflect on how people inside the club see it.

From their point of view, PERHAPS they believe they were doing what elite competitors do: looking at the rules, finding the limits, challenging interpretations and moving faster than the regulatory system.

From the outside, you might look at that and say, “That’s cheating.” From inside the organisation, they might say, “We found something nobody had thought of.”

If you believe you’ve found a way to bring money in, more or less within the rules (and the commission said it was not in the rules and it was cheating), you might tell yourself you’re just being a sharp competitor.

We are all asking “did City cheat?”. But I find this question interesting too: “how did City come to believe they weren’t?”

And understanding a mindset, or trying to, isn’t excusing it.

‘World’s Largest Time Capsule’ opened after 50 years... 

In 1977, a Boy Scout troop in Seward, Nebraska, created one of the most unusual time capsules of the era. Instead of burying letters or small artifacts, they entombed a brand-new 1977 Chevrolet Vega, along with period items such as soda bottles, newspapers, and a small motorcycle. The project, organized by Troop 256, reflected both the optimism of the late 1970s and the fascination with preserving contemporary culture for future generations.

The car itself, priced at just over $3,000 according to the original dealer sticker, was sealed in a concrete vault, wrapped in protective plastic, and surrounded by memorabilia meant to capture the spirit of the time. The walls were decorated with Scout troop names and painted murals, giving the capsule the feel of both a monument and a playful experiment in historical preservation.

You owe the IRS $100,000

They'll take $5,000 and close your file. Permanently. Balance goes to $0

It's called an Offer in Compromise. Form 656. The IRS approved 42% of them last year. Application fee: $205

Here's the exact formula they use to decide your number and how to reverse-engineer the lowest possible offer

The IRS doesn't want to chase you for 10 years. Liens require court filings. Levies require processing. Garnishments require administration. They'd rather take your $5,000 check today than spend a decade trying to squeeze $100,000 out of someone who will never have it

They literally built a math formula to calculate the minimum they'll accept. Here it is:

RCP = (monthly disposable income x remaining collection months) + (net realizable equity in assets)

Monthly disposable income: your gross monthly income minus IRS-allowed living expenses. They don't use YOUR actual expenses. They use standardized tables published on the IRS website. These tables set exact allowances by county for housing, food, transportation, healthcare, and out-of-pocket expenses

If you earn $4,200/month and the IRS allowable expense table for your county totals $3,900, your disposable income is $300/month. If you earn $3,800/month and the table allows $3,900, your disposable income is negative and the IRS considers it $0

Remaining collection months: for a lump sum offer (paid in 5 months or less), multiply disposable income by 12. For a periodic payment offer (paid over 6-24 months), multiply by 24. A lump sum offer will always be cheaper than a payment plan offer. Always choose lump sum if you can

Net realizable equity in assets: bank accounts, investments, vehicles, real property. BUT they subtract allowances. Household furnishings: exempt. Retirement accounts: heavily discounted, because the IRS applies a "quick sale value" and knows cashing them out triggers penalties and taxes

Real calculation:

Income: $4,200/month
IRS allowed expenses: $3,900/month
Disposable income: $300/month

Lump sum multiplier: 12 months
$300 x 12 = $3,600

Assets:
Bank account: $2,100
Car equity: $4,800 (below the IRS allowance, counts as $0)
Household goods: exempt

RCP: $3,600 + $2,100 = $5,700

Your offer: $5,700 on $100,000 in tax debt. 5.7 cents on the dollar

The nuclear part:

While the offer is being reviewed (6-24 months), collection activity legally stops. No levies. No wage garnishment. This is in IRC Section 6331(k)(1)

And if the IRS fails to make a determination within 24 months of receiving your application, your offer is AUTOMATICALLY ACCEPTED. Two years of silence = you win by default. IRC Section 7122(f)

The forms you need:

Form 433-A (OIC): complete financial disclosure. Every bank account, every asset, every income source, every expense. Fill it out accurately because they cross-reference it against bank and DMV records. Lying on this form is a federal crime

Form 656: the actual offer. Your amount, your payment terms, your signature

$205 application fee (waived if your income is low enough. the form has the table)

Initial payment with the application: 20% of your offer for lump sum. On a $5,700 offer that's $1,140

The variety is called Dickinson, the same species as butternut, and Libby's grows it by the thousands of acres around its cannery in Morton, Illinois.

Libby's makes about 85% of the canned pumpkin in the country and doesn't hide any of this. Nestle's own harvest release names the variety and says outright that pumpkin is a form of squash.

Harry loses a bet and asks Malfoid to the Yule Ball.

It started, as many of Harry’s worst ideas did, with Fred and George Weasley.

"You haven't asked anyone," Fred said, as if this were news.

"He hasn't asked anyone," George agreed, "because the only person he wants to ask is going with Diggory.”

Harry told them to shut up. He was in the common room. Ron was practising looking like a person who would rather die than wear dress robes. Hermione had a book open and was not reading it.

"Tell you what," said Fred. "A Galleon says you won't ask Malfoid."

"Which Malfoy?" said Ron, alarmed.

"There's only one at school, Ronald. Do keep up."

"I'm not asking Malfoy," said Harry.

"Malfoid," said George, pleasantly. "That's the bet. You don't. We collect. You do — well. Then you've got a partner, haven't you? Everybody wins. Except you, probably."

"She's not going to say yes."

"Then you've lost nothing," said Fred. "Go on. Champion's privilege. The worst she can do is hex you, and she does that on Tuesdays anyway."

Harry should have refused, but he was anything but a coward.

He found her in the library, after asking around a bit, which would have been embarrassing were it not assumed he was looking for a fight. She sat at a table in the corner by a window. Her pale hair was pulled back so tightly it seemed to lift the pointed bones of her face. She was alone. That was the first piece of luck. The second was that she looked up before he could lose his nerve.

She sighed and rolled her eyes. “What do you want, Potter?”

"I lost a bet," Harry said. "So let's get this over with. D'you want to go to the Yule Ball with me?"

She looked at him for a few seconds without changing her expression. Then she looked to the side. She appeared to be blushing.

“You must be desperate.” She attempted a laugh. “Is this some kind of joke, Potter? Me, going to the ball with a half-blood like you? Get real.”

“Alright, good,” he said firmly. He turned to leave before she could humiliate him any further.

“Yes,” she proclaimed with an upward lilt, as if she had surprised herself.

He stopped in his tracks. “What?” He almost raised his voice too loud for the library before turning around to look at her again. She had a mischievous smile.

“Yes.”

“Why,” Harry asked, exasperated. This was not what he expected.

“Why? Because I can’t resist the opportunity to torture you. I am going to embarrass you, if you are even brave enough to follow through.”

Harry sputtered. “What? You can’t find a date?” It was his best attempt.

“Oh I could. I have been asked many times already. I have no interest in those inferior specimens. The Malfoys have standards, you see. But I will make an exception for you, because this is just irresistible.”

He stood there, speechless. He looked out the window. Before he could come up with a response, she picked up her book and stood up. She walked over to him, grabbed his tie, and pulled him close, staring him down with malevolent eyes.

"Eight o'clock on Christmas Day. Dress robes. Not a Muggle dinner jacket. Not whatever the Dursleys think is formal. If you arrive smelling of broom polish I shall hex your shoes together and let you open the dance like that. Do we understand each other?"

Before he could come up with a response, she walked away.

…

"You asked her."

"That was the bet."

"You asked her and she said yes."

Ron was pacing around the room. Seamus and Dean were laughing it up.

"She's going to hex you," Ron said. "That's the game, that is. She says yes, you show up, she hexes you in front of four schools and tells her father you begged."

"She already said she'd hex me. That part's settled. It's only if I step on her toes or dress like a Muggle."

"You are Muggle-raised," Ron said, as if this had only just become legally relevant. "What does she think dress robes are? You can't wear trousers from the Dursleys, Harry. She'll know. They've got a look.”

Hermione, when they took it downstairs, pinched the bridge of her nose.

"Fred and George," she said.

"Fred and George," Harry agreed.

"And she said yes."

"She said yes, and then she said a lot of other things."

Hermione was quiet for a moment.

"Wear your green dress robes," she said at last. "The ones from Madam Malkin. Not a tie. Not Dudley's anything. If she tries to pull something nasty don’t let her get away with it."

“Right,” he replied. He had no idea what that meant.

Fred and George, passing the portrait hole with the satisfied air of men who had invented Christmas, flipped him a Galleon.

"Don't spend it before she kills you," said Fred.

"Buy a card," said George. "Something tasteful."

Harry told them to get stuffed. He put the Galleon in his pocket anyway.

….

The green robes made him look, he thought, like a Christmas tree that had learned shame. Harry checked his shoes three times. They were the same shoes.

"If she hexes you," Ron said, struggling into maroon velvet and a quantity of lace that history would not forgive, "I'll — I'll do something. I don't know what. Don't look at me like that. I'm in this."

By ten to eight the entrance hall was a crush of dress robes and panic. Parvati went by in shocking pink and gold and did not look at Harry at all, which he deserved. He had spent two weeks looking as if he might ask her and then asked the worst person in Slytherin for a Galleon.

"Potter."

He turned.

Malfoid was on the marble stairs.

She wore a black dress. Her hair was down. She even had makeup on. Harry’s stomach did a flip. The weirdest part was, she was smiling at him. And it wasn’t a mischievous grin, like her usual sadistic glee. She looked like she was happy to see him. But she quickly changed her expression, as if she remembered, to one of disdain.

"Green," she said. "Acceptable. Not Muggle. You may keep your toes for the present."

She stepped down and took his arm, with surprising ease. "Do not grin. You look simple when you grin. We are going in. If you tell anyone this was a bet I will kill you."

"It was a bet."

"I know it was a bet, Potter. I would not have said yes to a sincere request. Do not flatter yourself.”

…

The house tables were gone. In their place stood a crowd of smaller ones, each with a lantern that burned without smoke. The walls were covered in silver frost. Overhead the usual black, starry ceiling had been crossed with garlands of mistletoe and ivy.

It seemed like everyone turned to look as they came in, and whispered to each other.

Malfoy’s fingers tightened once on his sleeve and then went loose, as if she had remembered an audience.

"Breathe," she said, barely moving her mouth. "If you faint I shall leave you on the floor.”

"I'm not going to faint."

McGonagall met them before they could sit down. She looked at Harry. She looked at Malfoy. Several decades of House warfare passed behind her eyes and sat down, exhausted.

"Potter. Miss Malfoy. You will line up with the other Champions after the meal. I expect decorum."

"Yes, Professor," said Malfoy, with only a slight hint of sarcasm.

McGonagall's mouth thinned.

"The robes will do," she told Harry. "Try to remember, a waltz is not a tackle."

She swept off.

"She likes you," Malfoy said. "How unaccountable."

They were seated next to Cedric and Cho of course, at the Champion’s table. Starting the torture already, Harry thought. Krum arrived last with a girl Harry did not recognise for three full seconds as Hermione. Periwinkle blue. Hair up. Ron looked at Harry with wide eyes. Harry just shrugged, as if to say: “What of it?”

Cho smiled at Harry as if she were sorry and not sorry. Cedric poured pumpkin juice like a man determined to be decent.

"Didn't know you two were—" Cedric began, and stopped, which was why people liked Cedric.

"We aren't," said Harry and Malfoy together.

They looked at each other.

“I lost a bet,” she said suddenly, smiling. Harry just shook his head. She stole his excuse. Typical.

Neither Cedric nor Cho seemed to know if she was serious, or how to respond.

Dinner arrived and passed without a major incident, besides that Malfoid was making faces across the room, playing it up.

"You're enjoying this," Harry muttered.

"I enjoy winning. It is not the same as enjoying you." She narrowed her eyes as she set the goblet down. "Do not look at Granger like that. It is a hair potion and a neckline. We manage it before breakfast."

"She's my friend."

"I know. It is one of your more baffling hobbies. It is quite beneath you.”

Was that a compliment? Harry just sighed. There was no point in arguing. She only wanted to get a rise out of him.

Suddenly it was time for the dance.

Harry stood. His chair shrieked on the floor. Malfoy stood up smoothly, as if chairs had never misbehaved in her life. She put her hand in the air and waited for him to take it, sighing with irritation.

Her palm was cold in his hand.

They walked to the floor and waited for the music to start.

"If you make a mistake I will kill you. If you look at Chang I will kill you. If you count, count silently. If you talk, do not talk about Quidditch,” she whispered.

"You're nervous."

"I am Slytherin. I am never nervous. I am prepared."

Harry put his hand at her waist as the music started to play. He thought he could see a glisten of sweat on her forehead. He used to tease her about her forehead for being much too big. Undeniably, however, she looked absolutely beautiful that night.

Despite all his practice, it felt completely different in front of everyone, and with Malfoy no less. She was quietly counting as they stepped. Whether it was for his sake, or because she was afraid he would embarrass her, he wasn’t sure.

"You can close your mouth," she murmured. "You have fallen off a broom in front of the whole school. This is only dancing."

"You're counting."

"I am not."

They turned. Mistletoe swam. Ron's face went by, maroon and betrayed. Pansy went by, personally wounded. Snape, at the staff table, looked as if he had bitten a fork.

"Your Head of House wants me dead," Harry said.

"He wants a great many people dead. You will have to queue." A pause. Her voice dropped, unwilling. "You are not as catastrophic as I expected."

"Thanks."

"It was not a compliment. I am, against my better judgement, not hexing you."

"Yet."

"Do not make suggestions."

The dance ended before he had decided whether to bow. Cedric bowed. Krum nodded the way Krum did everything. Harry let go of her waist.

"Well," she said. "Your twins may keep their Galleon. I am going outside. I am tired of being stared at. Besides, it is much too warm here."

For some reason, Harry went after her.

…

He thought he had lost her, when he saw her through a frosted window.

She stood outside, leaning on the balcony, despite the fact that it was snowing and she was wearing only a dress. She clutched herself in her arms, clearly freezing.

"You followed me."

"You walked off before we had time to bow.”

"I said yes to a dance. I did not say yes to stay until midnight." She did not turn. "Go back in. Granger will want to lecture you on fraternising. She has her hair up. She will be unstoppable."

“It is freezing out.”

She didn’t respond, but her body was shivering.

He almost put his robe around her shoulders, but thought better of it.

"Why'd you say yes?" he asked.

"You asked."

"That's not a reason. You could've said no. You do that all the time."

She tilted her head up, looking up at the stars.

“I told you already. I like to see you squirm.”

She came up to him slowly, wrapping her arms around his shoulders. He flushed, not knowing how to react. He could hear his heart beating in his chest. She just looked into his eyes, smiling with glee. For some reason beyond himself, he thought of kissing her.

“Besides, I couldn’t stand to see you go with that Patil-girl. Totally beneath you.” She remembered herself suddenly and added “For a half-blood, anyway.”

"You're a real piece of work, Malfoid."

“Don’t call me that!” she said, forcing a pout. She stepped back, pretending to be upset, but she could not hide from him the impression that she enjoyed it somehow. She went back to leaning on the railing, looking out, as if that would be the end of it.

He leaned against the railing right next to her. It was only fair that he got his revenge now.

"I didn't step on your toes," Harry said.

"Do not fish."

“Since I did a good job, I think you owe me another dance.”

She paused, and then burst out into laughter, almost maniacal. It caught him by surprise.

“I don’t owe you anything.”

Harry took that for a no. He turned to leave.

“Are you coming inside? You’ll catch a cold.”

Suddenly she grabbed his left arm and hooked her arm under it.

"You may have one more dance," she said. "After that I am returning you to that rotten Weasley boy. If you tell anyone funny stories about what happened tonight you will not wake up the next morning.”

He couldn’t help but laugh at her idle threats. The rumors about them were already spreading and there was nothing to do about it now. Hell, he wouldn’t be surprised if they made the front page of the Daily Prophet. They made a striking couple, he had to admit. But he didn’t say anything about it, lest she change her mind.

When they got back into the ballroom, everyone was dancing. Thankfully, hardly anyone noticed them come in. She grabbed his hand, and put the other hand onto her waist.

They danced for a while without speaking. Harry hoped that nobody noticed when she laid her head on his shoulder and sighed.

“You are quite serviceable for a half-blood. I think I will keep you.”

My ‘baby’ turned 21 this week.

Born 11 weeks early, weighing just a few pounds.

I still remember the paediatrician coming to see us after I went into early labour at 28 weeks. He gave us a long list of things that could go wrong in neonatal intensive care.

Worst case: she might not come home at all.

This is the first time I held her - a few days after she was born. A rare few moments without the ventilator. Afterwards, she would need help to breathe for many weeks to come.

Although I look happy here, my heart was broken. And I was full of fear. Any mother would be.

Infertility, ectopic pregnancy and baby loss were part of my story too - along with premature birth and everything that followed.

No exam result or professional achievement will ever rival this moment -  bittersweet as it was.

Which is why I refuse to be erased - or to see other women erased - from the language we use to describe what our bodies are made to do.

Not every woman wants to have a baby. Not every woman is able to.

But women should not have to disappear from the language of pregnancy, birth and our own bodies in order for others to feel included.

Which is why I say no to “birthing people”, “menstruators”, “cervix havers” and every other reductive term for women.

There is nothing inclusive about making women disappear.

Under Indian Railways rules, a platform ticket is valid strictly for 2 hours from the time of issue. Once this 2-hour window expires, the holder is treated as a person travelling without a ticket. Consequently, the Travelling Ticket Examiner (TTE) is legally mandated to levy a minimum penalty of ₹500 (plus the cost of a platform ticket, making it roughly ₹510–₹520) for ticketless presence in the station area.

The Indian Railways Commercial Manual does not provide any provision for the automatic extension of a platform ticket's validity, even if the train is significantly delayed by the railways itself.

Legally, TTEs and station staff do not have the regulatory authority to waive fines or grant exemptions based on operational delays. The system operates on a rigid interpretation: if you are on the platform after 2 hours without a valid train travel ticket, you are in technical violation.

This rule helps manage station crowds, improve security, and prevent unauthorized long-term loitering. A platform ticket allows you to enter the station to see off or receive family, but it does not grant permission to travel or stay indefinitely.

McDonald's is spending 8.5 billion dollars to find out why families stopped coming.

I can save them the 8.5 billion.

They took out the playground.

The plan, announced Wednesday at investor day. Better food, faster service, new equipment, AI tools, hospitality training, and a bigger push into chicken and beverages. They call it Next. The goal, they say, is making customers feel more comfortable.

Wall Street loved it so much the stock fell 5 percent to its lowest since 2022.

Over five years McDonald's shares are down 3 percent. Burger King's parent is up 14. The owner of Taco Bell and KFC is up 13.

This is not a hamburger problem. This is a McDonald's problem.

So let us talk about who used to eat there.

Parents. That was the whole business. Parents at 5:40 on a Tuesday with three kids in the back and nothing thawed at home.

You did not go for the burger. You went because your kids could run screaming through a plastic tube for 40 minutes while you sat with a coffee and experienced silence.

That was the product. The food was the cover charge.

The first PlayPlace opened in 1971 in Birmingham, Alabama, and for fifty years it did one job. It made small children demand to go to McDonald's.

Then 2020 arrived, every play area in the country closed, and a great many never came back. The equipment came out during a remodeling program named Experience of the Future.

The Experience of the Future turned out to be a touchscreen.

Their own chief executive said he did not know if ball pits were in their future.

Sir, you were not selling ball pits. You were selling forty minutes.

So now there is no counter, no playground, and no reason for a seven year old to want to go. A screen, a window, and a bag.

And for that we pay prices that require a moment of reflection in the parking lot.

For thin, overcooked, oddly uniform pucks that taste like a memory of beef.

I did not love them because they were good. I loved them because I was eight and there was a slide.

And have you seen the new buildings.

The old ones were unmistakable. Red roof, yellow arches, legible from a highway at 70 to a child who could not yet read.

The new ones are a flat gray box with a small logo and a drive through wrapped around it. A regional claims office with a fryer.

They removed the color, the characters, the counter, and the playground, and then hired consultants to find out why it no longer feels like anywhere.

Which is why, when I have to eat fast food, I go to Chick-fil-A.

Not for the politics. For the competence.

They have led the customer satisfaction index for fast food eleven years running, and average 8.5 million dollars per location against McDonald's 4 million.

More than double, while closed on Sundays. Fifty two days a year with the lights off, and still double.

A seventeen year old hands you a bag and says my pleasure and means it about 70 percent, which is 70 percent more than a touchscreen has managed.

McDonald's is spending 8.5 billion on hospitality training.

Chick-fil-A earns 8.5 million per restaurant by just having some.

So here is my consulting proposal, free of charge, on behalf of mothers everywhere.

Put the playgrounds back.

Not a nostalgia campaign. Not a retro cup. The structure. Tubes, slides, a door the kids cannot open from the inside, and a bench where a tired woman can sit.

And understand what you are buying, because it is not lunch.

A six year old does not know your food is bad. He has no basis for comparison and no functioning palate. He thinks the burger is incredible because he is standing in a castle made of tubes.

That is the window. That is the only window you get.

You catch them before the taste buds arrive, and thirty years later they drive past your sign, feel something they cannot explain, and pull in anyway.

That is not a menu strategy. That is imprinting, and you shut it down in 2020 to save on cleaning.

Eight and a half billion dollars for AI tools and hospitality training.

Or a slide.

As I promised, I decided to recount, in the first person and directly, the circumstances surrounding the last training camp of the National Team.

At the end of the competition, already on the flight back from the United States, the President of the Federation asked and insisted that I reconsider the decision to leave, because the FPF wanted me to continue.

Right afterwards he asked me for my opinion on the name of the current head coach, which he was considering alongside other names he did not reveal to me.

I told the President of the Federation that, in my opinion, it would be the right choice.

That is why, on the day the current head coach was presented, I was genuinely happy with the choice. It was the right option, as the results are confirming.

A few days later I received a first contact from the new national team coach saying he would like to meet me in person. I said yes and we scheduled it for the end of my holidays.

We met at the Cidade do Futebol, where my club was holding its pre-season training camp.
That day the coach told me he was counting on me and that my presence was fundamental to his project. He presented me, right there, with a plan for my participation. He told me I would play the first match and the last one, and that for reasons of physical management he would always make three to four changes per match.

At that point he raised the possibility of me not travelling with the national team to Norway and Denmark. He proposed that I play the first match and stay in Portugal, then rejoin before the match at the Dragão.

I refused this proposal immediately. It seemed obvious to me that I could not accept it. It was not because I would not play the matches abroad that I would stop captaining our team. That privilege of staying in Portugal would not be a good example.

The coach ended up agreeing with my analysis.

This conversation was attended by Simão Coutinho, sporting director of Al Nassr, the person to whom the current coach reported throughout last season and one of those responsible for his signing by the club in 2025.

On the eve of the start of the camp the coach came to my house in Lisbon, at his request, for another conversation with me. The conversation was calm and all the principles agreed in August were maintained.

I played the match at Alvalade and, although substituted, I made no problem of it. I put the armband on Bruno Fernandes myself, far from imagining that I might be taking my last steps as a player and captain of the National Team. What mattered to me that day was our victory. Winning is always good; in Portugal and for my country, even better.

At lunchtime on the day of the match in Norway, an assistant to the coach came to the table where the group was having lunch and informed me that the coach wanted to speak to me.

To my absolute surprise, the coach asked me if I was fit to play 30 minutes. I was fully focused on my physical recovery, integrated with my teammates as always, and thinking that I would not play that day. Without any problem.

This request was something outside my physical recovery and training plan — because I was only going to play on the 4th at the Dragão — but of course I said yes. He replied that I should then be ready because I would play 30 minutes.
The rest everyone knows. I warmed up from half-time, watched the minutes go by, and was not called.

The coach had broken his word to me.

The Cancer Cells That Changed Their Minds

A KAIST team just reversed cancer without killing a single cell — and the method may matter more than the result.

For a century, oncology has had exactly one strategy: find the cancer and destroy it.

Chemotherapy poisons it. Radiation burns it. Surgery cuts it out. Immunotherapy teaches the body to hunt it. Every weapon differs in precision, but not in philosophy. The tumor is an enemy. You win by killing.

Now a team at South Korea's KAIST has proposed a heresy: *what if the tumor doesn't need to die?*

In a study led by Professor Kwang-Hyun Cho of the Department of Bio and Brain Engineering, published in Advanced Science ("Control of Cellular Differentiation Trajectories for Cancer Reversion," DOI 10.1002/advs.202402132), researchers took colon cancer cells and — without poisoning, irradiating, or cutting them — turned them back into normal cells.

Not dead. Not damaged. Just normal again.

The tumors, grown in mice, shrank dramatically. The surrounding tissue was left intact, because there was never an attack to survive.

This is early research — cell lines and animal models, no human trials, real obstacles still unsolved. But the conceptual break is the story. For the first time, cancer treatment has a second verb. Not just destroy. Also: convert.

The digital twin of a cell

The KAIST team's insight begins with a redefinition of what cancer is.

The conventional view treats cancer as a pile of broken machinery: mutations accumulate, checkpoints fail, cells proliferate. Cho's group looked at the same evidence and saw something different — a trajectory. During oncogenesis, they observed, normal cells don't just break. They regress, sliding backward along the differentiation path they followed when they matured. A colon cell becomes, in effect, a confused stem cell: immature, proliferative, lost.

If cancer is a wrong turn on a developmental road, then the treatment question changes. You don't blow up the road. You build a map and find the turn.

That map is what the team calls a digital twin — a complete computational model of the gene network governing a cell's differentiation. Using data from 4,252 intestinal cells, they reconstructed a network of 522 interacting components, capturing how genes regulate one another as a cell matures or degrades.

Then they did the audacious thing: they asked the simulation which levers, flipped together, would push a cancer cell back down the road toward normalcy.

The answer came through a system they built called BENEIN (Boolean Network Inference and Control), which models gene interactions as logical relationships and systematically tests which interventions redirect the network's state. The simulation pointed to three master regulators — the genes MYB, HDAC2, and FOXA2 — acting together as the switch that holds the cancerous state in place.

Turn all three off simultaneously, the model predicted, and the cell would stop proliferating and differentiate into something resembling a normal intestinal cell.

They tested it, and it worked.

In three colon cancer cell lines, suppressing MYB, HDAC2, and FOXA2 together strongly induced differentiation into normal-like cells. The cancer cells began expressing markers of healthy intestinal tissue. Proliferation collapsed — not because the cells died, but because they grew up.

In animal models, tumors formed from the reprogrammed cells were dramatically smaller than controls, and under the microscope they looked far more like normal tissue. The signature achievement, and the one that would matter most to any patient reading this: there was no collateral damage. Nothing was poisoned, burned, or irradiated. The healthy tissue never came under fire, because there was no fire.

Electric vehicles are not that green—or clean.

An EV enters the world carrying a heavy carbon debt—typically 40% to 70% higher manufacturing emissions than a conventional petrol or diesel vehicle.

This footprint is driven by the mad rush for energy-intensive mining and refining of lithium, cobalt, and nickel. On grids still powered by coal and gas, clearing that initial carbon deficit can take 60,000 to over 100,000 kilometres of real-world driving. It is a long-term gamble on vehicle longevity.

The theoretical models are upbeat. They promise the world: the battery will last, the grid will decarbonise, the weather will stay mild, and the owner will never encounter a structural or electronic defect. Beyond the showroom, however, practical setbacks mount quickly.

While home charging adds directly to household power bills, fast-charging outside major metropolitan corridors remains invisible. For a tradesman towing a trailer or driving rural routes, the extra battery weight and reduced range under load make every long trip a serious logistical exercise.

EVs currently bypass the federal fuel excise that traditional motorists pay, despite carrying significantly heavier battery packs that increase road wear and tear.

High-voltage battery packs are exceptionally costly. Minor accidents or cell degradations can trigger a $10,000 to $25,000 battery replacement, which usually means the car is a total write-off. Because the battery is the car, a viable second-hand EV market remains doubtful.

Electrification is not the frictionless or flawless successor to liquid fuels we were promised. Treating an evolving technology as an immediate, settled victory ignores substantial physical and economic realities.

These unfortunate surprises will be borne by the well-intentioned people who actually buy them, then have to run and repair them.

Ground beef in an American supermarket is now legally allowed to be part mushroom, and you will not find that on the front of the pack.

The blend is roughly seventy beef, thirty fungus. Some versions run pea protein instead, or alongside. The mushroom is chopped fine, hydrated, and mixed through the trim until the texture and the colour match, and it matches well, because that is the entire engineering problem and it was solved years ago. It goes in the same tray. It sits in the same case. It carries a leaf and a word like blended, and blended is doing a great deal of work.

Ground beef passed six dollars a pound in June for the first time on record. Beef and veal are forecast up 10.7 percent this year. The US cattle herd is at its lowest level in over seventy years and nobody expects relief before 2028. Ground beef is close to 48 percent of all the beef Americans eat.

So the chains had two options. Charge what the beef costs and watch the shopper reach for chicken. Or cut it with something that costs a fraction of it, hold the shelf price, and keep the item in the basket.

They went into the grinder because the grinder is the one place the eye cannot audit. A ribeye declares itself. Grain, marbling, fat cap, all of it visible, and nobody has ever tried to put a mushroom in one because you would find it in a second. Grind the same animal and the evidence disappears. Every food fraud in the record has gone the same route: the sausage, the pie, the patty, the ready meal. Horse turned up in mince and lasagne in 2013 and never once in a joint.

The cruelty of the timing is that American ground beef should be the best it has been in fifty years. Cattle are being fed to record weights, an average of 1,475 pounds live in March, because heavier animals are the only way to hold production up with fewer head. Heavier cattle carry more fat. More fat means richer trim going into the grinder.

The product was improving at the exact moment they started diluting it.

And swap out that thirty percent and look at what leaves. Thirty percent less B12, less heme iron, less zinc, less complete protein, replaced by water bound into fungal fibre. You are buying the same weight and taking home less food.

The blend was designed when beef was cheap and it was sold then as a choice for the planet. It is landing now because beef is dear, and not one word on the front of the pack has changed. The justification moved with the price, which tells you what the justification was.

Ground beef was the last part of the animal a family could still afford whole.

That is exactly why it went first.

This photo was taken in 1903 inside the Bryant & May match factory in Bow, East London.

Look at the young women's faces. Their jaws are swollen, rotting, glowing in the dark. They are teenagers — 14, 15, 16 years old. This disease was called "Phossy Jaw."

Their job was dipping matches into white phosphorus. White phosphorus is poison. Every day they breathed it. First their teeth fell out. Then their gums turned green and black. Then their entire jawbone rotted and had to be cut out by a doctor with no painkiller. Some died screaming.

The factory owners knew. They knew since 1880 that white phosphorus kills. But it was cheap. Safer red phosphorus cost 3 times more. So they kept using white.

These girls worked 14 hours, 6 days a week, for 4 shillings. If they talked, they were fined. If they dropped a match, they were beaten. Their faces glowed at night from the phosphorus — they called them "ghosts" on the streets of London.

In 1888, 1,400 of them went on strike. All teenagers. Led by a 16-year-old girl named Sarah Chapman. They marched to Parliament with their swollen faces and said: "We would rather starve than rot."

London was shocked. And finally, in 1908, Britain banned white phosphorus — because of these girls.
This was not medieval times. This was 1903 in London, the richest empire on earth.

They were just teenage girls working in a factory… but their courage forced an entire nation to change.

A Letter to All Players

Dear Miss Hunters,

We sincerely apologize for reaching out once again. Over the past several days, our team has been closely following your conversations and feedback across all platforms. For the issues that have surfaced since the announcement of Version 6.0—and the frustration these have caused our community—we want to clearly state: we are sorry.

As we've expressed before, our vision for Love and Deepspace has always been to build a world that grows alongside you—one that offers a richer, deeper sense of companionship over time.

As various issues have arisen in recent days, we have moved quickly to make the necessary adjustments. After reflecting on recent events, we recognize that we moved forward with the introduction of Valko before we were truly ready. In doing so, we let down the players who have supported us from the start, and we also fell short of delivering the experience that players anticipating Valko deserved. After extensive internal discussions, we have decided to make the following changes:

1. We have decided to cancel both the launch and any further development of the new love interest. We also commit that no additional love interests will be introduced in future content plans.

2. All other in-game systems and features originally scheduled for Version 6.0—including Home 2.0 and AR Photobooth—as well as the limited-time Selectable 5-Star Memory Rate-Up Event, will proceed as planned. The outfits, photo poses and scenes, and the Nighthush Box (the second-anniversary 4-Star Memory Selection Crate) originally planned as rewards for the Hunt in Linkon event will instead be sent to all players for free via in-game mail after the version update.

3. Going forward, the entire team will focus on further developing the stories and long-term companionship experiences of our five existing love interests, while ensuring a stable pace of Main Story production and updates. Rafayel's new Solar-Slot Memories and Companion will be revealed in July. Farspace Colonel Caleb and Onychinus Leader Sylus will also return in their Main Story branches in September and November, respectively. By participating in the relevant events, players will be able to obtain the corresponding 5-Star Main Story Branch Memories for free. We will continue to devote all our care and effort to bringing you richer stories and game experiences.

4. Beginning today and continuing for 30 days, players who log in each day will receive one Deepspace Wish via in-game mail. Each mail will remain claimable for three days, for a total of 30 Deepspace Wishes. We hope this can offer some compensation for the disappointment and disruption caused by these adjustments.

To our community: once again, we apologize. Because of our actions, the joy you should have found in Linkon City became a source of distress, and the feelings you hold most dear were hurt. We are deeply sorry for the hurt and disappointment we have caused.

Love and Deepspace has always been about sharing love with you and protecting the love we all hold dear. That purpose has never wavered. Every step forward taken by the love interests and Linkon City—from its beginnings to where it stands today—has been shaped by your feedback, your passion, and your trust. It is your presence, care, and companionship that give this world its meaning, and us the strength and direction to move forward.

Over the past two and a half years, we've shared moments of joy and gratitude, as well as challenges and difficult times. Through every late night devoted to making this world better, it has been the moments you've shared in Linkon City—and the love and passion behind them—that have kept us going. We hope to continue walking this road with you, building a world where love can take root, grow, and bloom.

Going forward, we will work harder, listen more carefully, and do our utmost to honor the trust you have placed in us. We will stay focused on delivering the experience you deserve—one filled with love where every moment in Linkon City can once again become a joyful and treasured memory.

Linkon City will always be here for you.

Thank you—for your trust, your honest feedback and encouragement, and for being with us every step of the way. Your companionship has helped light the path ahead, and your faith in us has given meaning to every effort we make. Thank you for your love throughout this journey. It gives us the courage to keep moving forward. We hope to repay that love with even more and even better content in the days to come.

Many of the onshore wind farms along the coasts of the UK and Denmark are falling apart after only 10 years. 

A study reveals that energy contributions from wind farms begin to fall sharply after only 10 to 15 years, leaving the skeletons of steel and plastic blowing in the wind.

The economic analysis reveals the lifespan of an onshore turbine is not 20 to 25 years, as stated by the wind industry itself, supported by the UK Government.

This peer reviewed British study reveals that the energy production of onshore wind farms falls substantially as they get older, due to wear and tear. Energy and environmental economist, Professor Gordon Hughes (University of Edinburgh), carried out the statistical analysis of wind farm performance data in the UK and Denmark.

He concluded that load factors, like electricity generated as a percentage of capacity, declined a lot faster than expected, suggesting a baseline 10 to 15 year lifespan. This is when the technical life of most turbines crunch to halt, and become unprofitable to continue. Rising maintenance costs makes them uneconomical.

While the wind industry generally forecasts a 25-year lifespan, the data reveals a different reality about the viability of keeping them spinning so long. Many companies now 'repower' (replace old turbines with new ones) long before the 25-year target to maximise subsidies and output. This often ends the lifespan of the original hardware much sooner.
